cards.title: Ada Lovelace saw computing's future in 1843
cards.body:
In the 1830s, Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer that was never fully built. In 1843 Ada Lovelace, a mathematician and the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, translated an article about it by the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea and added her own notes, which ended up far longer than the article itself.

In Note G she laid out a step-by-step method for the engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program. More striking was her vision. Babbage saw a number cruncher; Lovelace saw that if symbols such as musical notes could be represented as numbers, the machine could manipulate them too, and might even compose music.

She also argued the engine could not originate anything, only do what it was told. Alan Turing later answered that claim directly when asking whether machines could think.
cards.example: Turing called it Lady Lovelace's Objection in his 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence. The same argument shows up today in debates about whether AI models are truly creative or just recombining their training data.
cards.takeaway: Lovelace saw that computers could manipulate any symbol, not just numbers.

cards.title: ROIC: the quality test for any business
cards.body:
Return on invested capital asks a simple question: for every dollar tied up in the business, how much profit does it earn? It's calculated as NOPAT, or net operating profit after tax, divided by invested capital, roughly the debt and equity funding the operating assets.

ROIC matters because growth only creates value when returns beat the cost of capital. A company earning 20% on capital that costs 9% creates value with every dollar it reinvests. One earning 6% destroys value as it grows, even while revenue and earnings rise.

Buy-side analysts look for businesses that sustain high ROIC for years, which usually signals a competitive advantage, and that still have room to reinvest at those rates. High ROIC with nowhere to reinvest is good; high ROIC with a long reinvestment runway is how compounders are made.
cards.example: A retailer has operating income of $500M and a 25% tax rate, so NOPAT is $375M. With invested capital of $2.5B, ROIC is 15%. If its cost of capital is 8%, each extra $100M reinvested at similar returns earns about $7M a year above what that capital costs.
cards.takeaway: Growth only creates value when ROIC is above the cost of capital.

cards.title: Sleep is the most legal performance drug
cards.body:
Sleep is when your body repairs muscle, consolidates the day's memories, and resets the hormones that regulate hunger and stress. Most adults need at least seven hours, and young adults often do best with more. Cutting sleep short hurts reaction time, mood, motivation and decision-making, and you're usually a poor judge of how impaired you are.

Athletes give a striking demonstration. In a 2011 Stanford study led by Cheri Mah, college basketball players aimed for ten hours in bed each night for several weeks. Their sprint times got faster and their shooting accuracy improved.

The basics are unglamorous but effective: consistent sleep and wake times, even on weekends; a cool, dark room; and no caffeine from the afternoon on, since its effects can linger for many hours. Consistency matters as much as total hours.
cards.example: If you aim to be asleep by 11:30 pm, cut off coffee by early afternoon and set an 11:00 pm phone alarm as a cue to start winding down. Keep the same wake time for a full week, Saturday included, and notice how your runs and lifts feel.
cards.takeaway: Consistent, sufficient sleep improves almost everything you care about.

cards.title: Chekhov's gun: every detail must earn its place
cards.body:
Anton Chekhov, the Russian playwright and master of the short story, gave writers a rule that has outlived him. In letters and conversations he made the point in several forms: if a story shows a rifle hanging on the wall in the first act, it must go off later. Otherwise, take it out.

The principle is about promises. Every detail a writer includes signals importance to the reader. Details that never pay off waste attention and erode trust, while ones that do create that satisfying click when the story comes together.

It applies far beyond fiction. In an essay, a stock pitch or a presentation, every chart, statistic and anecdote should advance your argument. If a slide doesn't change what your audience believes or does, it's an unfired gun, and it should be cut.
cards.example: Reread a recent assignment or cover letter and highlight every detail. For each one, ask what it sets up or proves. Anything that answers "nothing" gets cut. Most drafts get shorter and stronger in the same move.
cards.takeaway: If a detail doesn't pay off, it doesn't belong.

cards.title: Why ice floats, and why life depends on it
cards.body:
Nearly every substance is denser as a solid than as a liquid, so it sinks when it freezes. Water is a strange exception. As it cools below about 4°C, hydrogen bonds start locking its molecules into an open, hexagonal lattice that takes up more space. By the time it's ice, it's roughly 9% less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

This quirk shapes the planet. Lakes freeze from the top down, and the ice layer insulates the water beneath it. The densest water, at about 4°C, settles at the bottom, where fish survive the winter. If ice sank, lakes in cold climates could freeze solid from the bottom up.

The same expansion has a destructive side. Water seeping into cracks in rock or pavement expands as it freezes, prying them apart. That's a big part of how Canadian winters create potholes.
cards.example: Fill a plastic cup to the brim with water and freeze it overnight. The ice will rise above the rim, showing that expansion. It's also why a full glass bottle of water left in the freezer can crack.
cards.takeaway: Ice floats because water expands as it freezes, protecting life below.

cards.title: The Ship of Theseus: what makes you you?
cards.body:
The Greek writer Plutarch described a puzzle about the ship of the hero Theseus, preserved by the Athenians for generations. As its planks rotted, each was replaced with new timber. Eventually not one original plank remained. Was it still the same ship?

Thomas Hobbes added a twist: suppose someone collected all the old planks and rebuilt the original. Now there are two ships. Which one is the real Ship of Theseus?

The puzzle matters because it's about identity over time, including yours. Much of your body is renewed over the years, and your beliefs, tastes and friendships change. Some philosophers locate identity in continuity of form and function; others in psychological links like memory. It applies to institutions too: is a company the same company once every employee and product has changed?
cards.example: Consider a band that has replaced every original member, or a fund whose founder has retired and whose team has fully turned over. Investors face this question directly: is the track record still meaningful if the people and process behind it are gone?
cards.takeaway: Identity may live in continuity and pattern, not in the original parts.

quiz.question: What was Ada Lovelace's most far-reaching insight about the Analytical Engine?
options: It could be built from electrical circuits
It would replace human mathematicians
It could only perform addition
If symbols like musical notes were represented as numbers, it could manipulate them too
quiz.explanation: Babbage saw a calculator; Lovelace saw a general symbol-manipulating machine, the core idea of modern computing.

quiz.question: A company earns a 6% ROIC and has a 9% cost of capital. What happens as it reinvests to grow?
options: It creates value because revenue rises
It destroys value, because each reinvested dollar earns less than it costs
Nothing, since ROIC doesn't affect value
It creates value as long as earnings grow
quiz.explanation: Growth only creates value when returns exceed the cost of capital; at 6% vs 9%, every dollar reinvested loses value.

quiz.question: What did Cheri Mah's study find when basketball players extended their sleep?
options: Sprint times got faster and shooting accuracy improved
Players gained weight but performed the same
Performance dropped from oversleeping
Only reaction time changed
quiz.explanation: Aiming for ten hours in bed for several weeks improved both speed and shooting.

quiz.question: In a stock pitch, what does following Chekhov's gun mean?
options: Open with your most dramatic statistic
Include every data point you found to show effort
Cut any chart or fact that doesn't advance your argument
Save your recommendation for the very end
quiz.explanation: Every detail should pay off; anything that doesn't support the thesis wastes your audience's attention.

quiz.question: Why do lakes freeze from the top down?
options: Wind cools the surface faster than the bottom
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats
Salt sinks to the bottom and prevents freezing
The lake bed heats the water from below
quiz.explanation: Water expands as it freezes, so ice floats and insulates the denser, roughly 4°C water beneath it.

quiz.question: What was Hobbes's twist on the Ship of Theseus?
options: The ship sank and was never found
Theseus refused to replace any planks
Plutarch made the story up
The old planks are rebuilt into a second ship, raising the question of which is the real one
quiz.explanation: With two candidate ships, it becomes much harder to say whether identity follows the parts or the continuity.
